summary.title: Rules for Writing Software Tutorials
summary.one_liner: You learn a set of concrete rules, with bad and good examples, for writing software tutorials that readers can follow and copy/paste without getting stuck.
keywords: how to write a software tutorial
takeaways: Write for beginners: avoid expert jargon and explain terms a newcomer would not know.
Make snippets copy/pasteable: omit shell prompts, use non-interactive flags, and chain commands with && so failures stop execution.
Separate user-defined values (environment variables, named constants with comments) from code that must stay unchanged.
Use unambiguous, realistic example values and keep example code in a working state so readers can build as they go.
Promise a clear outcome in the title, explain the goal early, and show the end result as soon as possible.
summary.summary: This long-form essay lists a series of rules for writing software tutorials, such as writing for beginners, promising clear outcomes in titles, and showing the end result early. Each rule is illustrated with a bad example and a rewritten good example, often using shell commands, Go, C, and SQL. The examples focus on copy/paste safety, long command-line flags, environment variables for user-defined values, and keeping code buildable at every step. The page also introduces the idea of teaching one thing per tutorial.
